prompt: What is the purpose of a 10-minute 'first pass' through a PL paper (title, abstract, motivating example, headings, conclusion)?
choices: To fully understand the paper's proofs before moving on
To decide the paper's category and whether it's worth a deeper read, without yet understanding the mechanism
To memorize the evaluation section's numbers for later citation
To identify every related-work citation the paper builds on

prompt: A PL paper states a theorem like 'well-typed programs don't get stuck.' Where should you look before trusting that this applies to the full language described in the paper's introduction?
choices: The abstract, since it always states the theorem's exact scope
The theorem's stated scope and premises in the metatheory section — it's often proved only for a minimal core calculus
The paper's title, which lists every construct the proof covers
The references section, since scope is established by citation count

prompt: Running a BPE tokenizer like tiktoken's cl100k_base on source-code identifiers, what pattern should you expect?
choices: Every identifier, regardless of length, encodes to exactly one token

Short, frequent identifiers (like `count`) tend to stay as one token, while long compound identifiers fragment into several subword pieces that don't reliably align with camelCase or snake_case boundaries
Identifiers are tokenized character-by-character, one token per character, with no merging at all
BPE tokenizers refuse to tokenize identifiers and fall back to a fixed 'UNK' token

prompt: In formal-language terms, why is generalizing to arbitrarily deep bracket nesting fundamentally hard for a fixed-depth Transformer, in a way it is not hard for your recursive-descent parser?
choices: Balanced-bracket matching (a Dyck language) is context-free, not regular, and requires unbounded stack memory to recognize in general; a parser's recursion supplies that stack via the call stack, while self-attention over a bounded number of layers only approximates counting/stack behavior and tends to degrade beyond the nesting depths seen in training
Transformers process tokens one at a time like an RNN, so they simply run out of time on long inputs
Bracket characters are extremely rare in BPE vocabularies, so the tokenizer drops them
Recursive-descent parsers don't actually handle nested brackets either, so the comparison doesn't apply

prompt: This module recommends which approach to tracking arXiv cs.PL over time?
choices: Read every paper in the listing in full, once a week, cover to cover
Read the field's single most-cited paper thoroughly, once, and consider that sufficient going forward
A lightweight standing habit: subscribe to the listing/RSS feed, skim more heavily around conference deadline windows, and keep a short triage log per paper
Wait until a paper is discussed on social media before ever opening it

prompt: Why can an AI coding assistant produce code that reads fluently but fails to typecheck or parse?
choices: Because its tokenizer strips out all type annotations before generation

Because it is trained as next-token prediction over a flat subword sequence with no structural rule enforcing invariants like matching brackets or type compatibility — fluency is a learned statistical pattern, not a guarantee the way a parser's grammar or a type checker's rules are
Because code LLMs do not have access to any programming language's keywords
Because type errors are impossible to represent as text, so the model never sees them during training

prompt: A PL paper's evaluation section reports '40% faster than the baseline' with no baseline implementation named, no hardware specified, and results from a single run. Per this module's approach to reading evaluations, what's the right response?
choices: Accept the number at face value since it appears in a peer-reviewed venue

Treat the number as unverifiable as stated and look for the missing methodology (named baseline, hardware, repeated runs with variance) before crediting the claim, the same scrutiny you'd apply to checking a theorem's stated scope
Reject the entire paper as fraudulent without reading further
Assume '40% faster' is a typo and the real number must be in an appendix

prompt: What did code2vec (Alon et al., POPL 2019) do differently from a standard flat subword tokenizer, specifically to give a model access to a program's grammatical structure?
choices: It ignored the AST entirely and trained only on raw byte sequences
It represented code as paths through the AST between pairs of leaf nodes, rather than as a flat sequence of subword tokens
It required every input program to already be fully type-annotated before training
It replaced identifiers with randomly generated placeholder names to remove structure
